title: Keeping Up with Science: Brain Cells That Keep You Motivated (B1)

elements.content: Welcome to Keeping Up with Science. Review the research context and metadata below:

Session Overview:
• Duration: 60 minutes
• Languages: 🇬🇧 English
• Level: Intermediate (B1)
• Theme: Neuroscience, Motivation, & Dopamine

What is your initial reaction when reading about this scientific study?
How might this discovery change how we understand daily health or technology?
Master the core scientific vocabulary and collocations for this topic (10 items):

items.definition: the reason or desires that compel someone to act.
items.example: Scientists discovered brain cells that control daily motivation.

items.definition: a specialized cell transmitting nerve impulses; a nerve cell.
items.example: Specific neural circuits fire when we initiate a tough task.

items.definition: a neural pathway in the brain.
items.example: Dopamine circuits regulate feelings of reward and drive.

items.definition: persistence in doing something despite difficulty.
items.example: Brain cells dedicated to perseverance help us finish long projects.

items.definition: a neurotransmitter associated with pleasure and motivation.
items.example: Dopamine release encourages repeated goal-oriented behavior.

items.definition: the firing or release of electrical activity in neurons.
items.example: Neuronal discharge increases when a reward is near.

items.definition: a thing that motivates or encourages one to do something.
items.example: Clear incentives activate brain circuits for action.

items.definition: extreme tiredness resulting from mental or physical exertion.
items.example: Overcoming mental fatigue depends on specific cell signaling.

items.definition: a thing or event that evokes a specific functional reaction.
items.example: A positive stimulus triggers neural drive to achieve goals.

items.definition: the ability to assess and initiate things independently.
items.example: Taking initiative requires strong neural activation.

elements.title: Grammar Explanation (Intermediate (B1))
elements.content:
Use relative clauses to describe scientific discoveries (e.g., Scientists discovered brain cells which regulate motivation).
🧩 Interactive Word Bank:
Tap a word chip below, then tap any empty bracket [_____] to place it!
which
that
who
relative clause
📝 Task 1 : Part A: Rule Formulation:
Complete the rule: Use 'who' for people, and _____ or _____ for cells, objects, and concepts.
📝 Task 1 : Part B: Structured Practice:
These are the neurons _____ keep you motivated during difficult tasks.
The scientist _____ led the research published the results in August.
It is a discovery _____ could help treat clinical apathy.

🗣️ Task 2 : Interactive Speaking:
Describe a personal habit that keeps you motivated during work.
A comparative reflection on our habits and self-perceptions.
Analyze the core scientific findings and discuss the personal prompts in pairs:

prompts: How does intrinsic motivation drive long-term academic and professional success?
What is the basic function of a neuron in transmitting chemical messages?
How does a neural circuit process external rewards and form daily habits?
Why is psychological perseverance essential when tackling difficult challenges?
What role does dopamine release play in feeling satisfaction after completing a task?
How does an electrical discharge between neurons create sensory experiences?
What financial or personal incentive encourages you to work harder?
How do you manage physical and mental fatigue after a hectic workday?
How does a positive visual stimulus trigger creative thinking in the brain?
Why is taking personal initiative important in modern competitive workplaces?

pairs.correct: The cells which / that control motivation.
pairs.note: Use 'which' or 'that' for non-human objects and cells, not 'who'.
